content.thinking:
I'm planning the capybara's proportions and whimsical design—chubby barrel body, blunt snout, tiny ears, facing forward with a bird perched on its head—then setting up the skeleton structure starting from the hips as root through the spine toward the neck and head.

Mapping out joint positions along the spine using a chain of catmull path points, then branching off a neck chain from the final spine joint to position the raised head and snout.

Neck join point lines up fine with spine's end. For the tail, since capybaras barely have one, I'll just add a tiny short stub chain from the hips as a small bump rather than a full tail. Then for the body mesh, I'm planning a loft along the spine stations using the bone chain, extending from the rump back past the spine start and up through the neck/head base, letting weights fall back to the nearest joint beyond the chain's ends.

Defining more loft stations...

For coloring, I'm setting up a cel-shaded mottled coat using a warm tan base and darker brown blotches, with a lighter shade for the belly.

For the fur, I'm scattering around 500 small tuft cards across the body surface, tinted by the coat color, leaning slightly backward and filtering out cards on the underside.

Now I'm working out the leg rig: four short thick legs with shoulder and foot positions defined, needing bend-adjusted limb lengths so the chain doesn't sit perfectly straight between joints.

Adding fur gradient with cel-shading wrapped around the coat colors, then building out feet with flattened sphere toe pads and ellipsoid foot pads in dark brown tones.

Now I'm adding tiny cone nails to the toes, attaching feet to the last bone joint in the leg chain, and checking that everything sits correctly above the floor plane. Moving on to lofting the head shape from base to snout using a series of scaled stations for width and height along the way.

For the capybara's blocky head, I'm thinking through whether to use a rounded skull plus a boxy snout or just extend the loft with more stations, then adding a dark nose pad sphere near the tip and double-checking the loft's rounded end cap doesn't make the snout stick out too far given the radius at the last station.

Adding nostrils as tiny dark spheres, then sweeping a curved catmull path for the mouth line to create a subtle smile shape beneath the nose.

Now I'm draping the mouth path onto the head surface so it inherits the skin weights correctly. For the jaw, I'm planning a separate lower jaw bone and joint, positioned under the mouth and parented to the head, with a cream-colored swept rod forming the chin geometry.

I'll add a small pale muzzle sphere for the chin and sketch in a couple tiny cream incisor boxes peeking beneath the mouth line, careful to size and place them so they stay hidden within the chin geometry rather than floating awkwardly.

Now for the eyes — positioning them high on the sides of the head like a real capybara, finding the surface point near that location and sticking a dark sphere there with a small white highlight sphere offset slightly above it for shine.

Adding ears next, placed as small flattened spheres near the top rear of the head, tilted outward with a darker coat color and a smaller pinkish-brown inner ear sphere offset forward for depth.

Now I'm figuring out where the bird perches on the crown of the head, between the ears, sitting around height 0.79 — the bird itself needs its own joint hierarchy with a body sphere, head sphere, beak cone, tail, wing sweeps, and thin leg rods with feet.

Legs lift the body slightly above the crown, so I'm positioning the body center and giving it an ellipsoid shape tilted so the breast points up and forward while the tail angles down-back, working through the rotation math to get that orientation right.

I'm picking a blue tit color palette—blue cap, blue wings, yellow breast, white face, dark eye stripe, dark beak, grey legs, olive back—then placing the head sphere just above the body and working out how to paint the cap color onto it.

Adding beak and eye details...

Still shaping wing geometry...

Now for the tail I'm flattening it into a rod that tapers, wide in X but thin vertically, tilted slightly downward to avoid clipping, colored dark blue with flat end caps. For the legs, I'm placing thin rods extending from the body's underside down toward where they should meet the head's crown height, adjusting the sink depth so they connect properly.

Legs embed about 5mm into the head, with tiny toe rods extending forward from the feet. I'm setting the body scale and center position, then starting on the head's position next.

Now I'm placing the beak and tail geometry relative to the head, and considering whether the head needs its own joint versus being part of the base bird joint chain—birdBase as root parent, birdHead positioned above it, with tail and wing roles assigned where appropriate. Moving on to the whiskers now, sketching thin radiating rods from the muzzle sides.

Skipping eyelashes, but adding subtle cheek blush as small flattened pink spheres stuck to the surface near the muzzle for a whimsical touch.

I'm scattering fur card tufts across the head and body, with denser tufts between the ears and on the cheeks. For coloring, I'm planning a blunt dark nose pad, a lighter tan belly versus darker mottled brown back, and a subtle darker streak along the spine using a grain texture for fur-like striping.

Building the countershaded coat color...

For cards I'll use the unshaded coat tint so texture reads independent of cel shading, blending with the tuft overlay for subtle variation. For the head I'm thinking through a gradient toward a lighter muzzle tone near the front of the face.

Setting muzzle to a slightly lighter tan, with a darker reddish-brown nose pad for character. Legs and feet get darker brown tones with even darker toes and nails. For the hind legs I want thicker hams, so I'm tapering the sweep radius along the leg chain to bulge at the hip and narrow toward the foot.

Working out the front leg radii similarly, then checking that the foot's sweep ends at a reasonable height so it doesn't sink below the ground plane. I'm adjusting the target y-position and limb segment lengths so the foot and toes land naturally without the leg appearing too short or bent awkwardly.

Now I'm considering the bend direction argument for the limb IK - deciding that front legs should bend elbow-backward while hind legs bend knee-forward to match a capybara's natural stance.

For the chain geometry, I'm working out that a three-point limb (root, joint, end) can be passed as a simple polyline rather than a smoothed curve, since the joint should remain sharp rather than rounded.

Now I'm figuring out leg placement: side flag determines x-offset sign, with front legs parenting to a spine joint and hind legs parenting to the hips. The hips themselves act as a structural joint with no mesh of their own, just serving as the parent anchor so the spine and hind legs move together correctly. I'm also planning a small tail stub chain parented to the hips.

For the tail I'm sweeping a tiny spike-shaped cone from a point near the rump to a tip slightly above and forward, using a single joint since the chain only has one span and one name. Then I'm adjusting the body proportions for a cute, rounded capybara silhouette—checking that the loft width, height, and rump cap radius work out so the rounded end doesn't push the body length too far.

I realize the total length is coming out too long (~1.5 vs capybara's actual ~1.2), so I'm compressing the z-coordinates and shifting the hips forward to around -0.5, then redefining a shorter set of body stations with adjusted widths and heights to get a more compact, proportionate shape.

Now I'm mapping out the spine chain and neck joints, then placing head stations tapering from width .34 down to .26 toward the snout tip, capping the length appropriately for a rounder, more compact head.

Working out the nose pad, nostrils, and mouth drape coordinates...

Still placing the jaw, chin, teeth, eyes, and ears relative to the head surface...

Adding the inner ear detail offset along the ear's rotated normal so it faces outward, then shifting to the bird placement — adjusting its z-coordinate to sit near the head's crown by offsetting previous values by about 0.12.

Working out whisker roots fanning from the muzzle, then shifting to foot placements—computing shoulder and hip joint positions for front and hind legs so the feet land at proper ground contact points.

Still working out paw details...

I'm thinking through whether fur cards should extend to the legs — probably skip for simplicity — and sketching out the body fur layout, roughly 420 cards sized small, using a teardrop strand texture drawn as overlapping SVG paths to mimic tufts.

Scattering those fur cards across the body with distance constraints and tuning size, lean, bend, and spin for natural variation, keeping triangle counts manageable. I'm doing the same for the head with fewer, smaller cards, filtering out the snout area and leaving room for cheek details.

Now setting up the surface calls for body and head meshes, applying countershaded tan tint cards, and skipping minor details like eye-rings and eyebrow tufts for simplicity. For the wing, adding a contrasting pale stripe sweep over the blue base, and planning a dark center line for the chest paint.

I'm deciding to skip the belly dark sweep and bib details, and assigning a "wing" role to the relevant joints. I'm also auditing my imports carefully to avoid unused variables, keeping only what's actually used like stripes for the wing pattern.

Now I'm setting up the module imports from the builder, IK, math, path, paint, and toon kits, and defining a helper function for creating small low-poly spheres to use for minor body parts.

Building the capybara's skeleton now, starting with the hips as the root joint and a spine chain extending forward, followed by a neck chain with its own joint positions.

I'm defining the head and body lofts with their bone bindings and colors, then placing eye spheres by finding the nearest surface point on the head loft and embedding sphere sticks there, inheriting bone weights from the skin.

I'm confirming the head crown height sits around .765 given the loft stations, then positioning the bird joints — base and head — stacked above the crown with a small offset so they sit naturally on top.

For the beak, I'm adding two small spikes off the bird head bone, an upper and lower one with different angles and thicknesses to suggest a beak shape, keeping it simple rather than a jointed jaw. Then I'm placing a tiny ink-colored eye sphere offset to the side and slightly forward on the head.

Now I'm shading the head with a countershade effect, blue on top transitioning to white underneath based on the surface normal, with the eye sitting near that color boundary. I'm also draping a stripe pattern across the head surface using a curved path of points swept with a thin ink-colored tube, bound to the bird head bone's default weights.

Moving to the body, I'm positioning and scaling a sphere for the torso, rotating it slightly, and applying a countershade paint with blue-grey and yellow tones to approximate a blue tit's coloring, adjusting toward a more realistic greenish mantle shade.

Now I'm defining the wing joints and sweep paths, positioning wingL and wingR relative to the bird's base with directional offsets and a tapering radius function along the wing's length.

Next I'm sketching the tail: a joint at the back-bottom of the body, with a two-point sweep tapering from thick at the base to narrow at the tip, using rounded-to-flat end caps for a natural feather shape.

Now I'm adding legs as simple rods attached to the base bone, then giving each foot three forward toes plus a back toe, all thin tapered rods in a muted brown. I'm leaving the cap ends flat and skipping any extra head tuft detail, then filtering fur cards by a z-depth cutoff to control which ones render near the head.

I'm excluding fur cards near the bird region using a positional check, setting the fur tint color for cards, and considering a small decorative flower but deciding against it since the reference doesn't have one. I'm also planning hind foot toenails and a leg gradient paint running from the coat base color into a darker brown, then checking the sweep function's type signature for the radius array and paint options.

For the limb function, I'm working out how it accepts root and target points with length arrays to build chains, and figuring out how to safely grab the tip joint from a leg's joint array, considering fallback options for when the tip property might be null.

Now I'm designing a foot function that attaches a padded sphere to the hand/ankle bone, then adds four toe spheres offset along the x-axis with varying positions and scales, plus small spike-shaped nails at the tip of each toe.

For whiskers I'm adding four per side attached to a bone head. For the mouth, I'm sweeping a smile curve generated from catmull points, drape-fitted to the head surface, into a dark colored tube to form lips. I'm also considering adding scattered dark dot spheres on the muzzle sides to represent whisker follicles.

Now I'm scattering small dark embedded spheres on the muzzle using filtered surface hits (constrained by z, y, x, and normal direction) to represent whisker dots, then moving on to writing the meta description fields and double-checking that all defined coordinate variables like hips and neck are actually used before starting the tuft SVG path.

Writing tuft SVG paths... Then I'm confirming the hips role passes correctly as "spine" in the joint options, and setting up the body loft with 12 sides before finalizing part names and writing the file.
